# On Small Moments

I've been thinking about how the best things in life rarely announce themselves. They slip past while you're distracted, checking your phone or mentally rehearsing tomorrow's conversation.

Last week, I noticed my neighbor watering plants on her porch at dusk. She wasn't rushing. The hose hung loosely in one hand while she talked to someone inside through the open door. Nothing remarkable—except everything was. The soft light, the patience in how she moved, the ordinary fact of her existence right there next to mine.

We live in a culture obsessed with peaks: the promotion, the wedding, the vacation. But life is mostly the in-between. It's the coffee that tastes slightly better on a particular Tuesday. It's the exact moment a song becomes your favorite. It's recognizing your own voice in a friend's laugh.

I think we've been sold a false bill of goods about meaning. We're told to optimize, to chase, to document everything so it counts. But maybe counting things is precisely how we lose them.

There's something liberating about accepting that most moments won't matter to anyone but you. You can smell rain without posting about it. You can change your mind about something you said last year without announcing the update. You can simply exist, occasionally delighted, mostly ordinary.

The days pass either way. We might as well notice them—not to make them special, but to realize they already are. That's enough. That has to be enough.
